summary: A mountain-woman figure whose representations range across threatening, maternal, and theatrical traditions.
description: Yamauba is not one stable biography but a mountain-woman figure whose narrative and visual meanings move between danger, wilderness, beauty, and care. The Metropolitan Museum of Art identifies an Utamaro print from about 1795 in which Yamauba and Kintarō appear as adoptive mother and son in an intimate domestic moment. A ColBase record reached through Japan Search explains how loose hair and a leaf-patterned robe still signal the supernatural mountain figure even when Utamaro renders her as a beautiful young woman. Read together, these works show Edo-period artists holding tenderness and unease within the same familiar identity.
traditionNotes: The maternal Ashigara association is one powerful strand rather than a complete definition. Institutional records also preserve the broader image of a frightening woman or ogress of the deep mountains, so the archive keeps nurturing and threatening registers visible together.

variants.label: Maternal pairing with Kintarō
variants.description: Utamaro produced multiple images of Yamauba and Kintarō that translate a supernatural mountain figure into intimate scenes of touch, feeding, conversation, and maternal attention.

variants.label: The dangerous mountain woman
variants.description: The wider name also carries the older, less domestic image of a devil woman or mountain ogress dwelling beyond settled space. This register should not be erased by the later mother-and-child pairing.

sourceNotes: This remains an artwork-grounded entry, not a complete survey of regional Yamauba traditions, performance history, or scholarship.

summary: An oni leader at the center of a famous demon-slaying tale associated with Minamoto no Yorimitsu and his retainers.
description: Shuten-dōji stands at the center of one of Japan’s enduring demon-slaying cycles, but the surviving story is neither singular nor fixed. In the familiar Mount Ōe sequence, Minamoto no Yorimitsu and his companions enter the oni stronghold disguised as travelling priests, use sake to incapacitate their host, and strike while he sleeps; even after decapitation, the severed head remains a final danger. Illustrated handscrolls turn the expedition into a sequence of crossings, disguises, feasting, combat, release, and return. A separate Ibuki-dōji cycle instead begins with the figure’s upbringing at Mount Ibuki before his movement to Mount Ōe, revealing how origin, geography, and identity shift across objects and periods.
traditionNotes: Mountains, origin episodes, names, divine interventions, and the ordering of events change across texts and images. The archive presents the Ōeyama expedition and Ibuki upbringing as connected variants rather than forcing them into one definitive biography.

variants.label: The Mount Ōe expedition
variants.description: Illustrated narratives follow Yorimitsu and his retainers through disguise, supernatural aid, the oni feast, Shuten-dōji’s intoxication and decapitation, and the dangerous flight of the severed head.
variants.period: Medieval tale tradition; later handscroll and print culture

variants.label: Ibuki-dōji upbringing

summary: An oni of linked but variable encounter cycles in which Watanabe no Tsuna severs an arm and the disguised figure later reclaims it.
description: Ibaraki-dōji emerges most vividly through pursuit, disguise, and reversal. A British Museum print by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi shows the oni escaping after taking back a severed arm while disguised as Watanabe no Tsuna’s elderly aunt. Curatorial commentary for another museum object preserves a different approach to the encounter: near Modoribashi, a beautiful woman named Ibaraki asks Tsuna for an escort, transforms, attacks him, and loses an arm to his sword. These objects do not supply one seamless chronology. Instead they reveal a figure repeatedly defined by unstable appearance, the vulnerability of a celebrated warrior, and the failure of physical victory to end a supernatural conflict.
traditionNotes: Gate, bridge, disguise, kinship identity, and the exact opponent vary across tellings and represented objects. This record limits itself to institutional descriptions that explicitly name Ibaraki and treats adjacent arm-retrieval tales as related rather than automatically identical.

summary: A Heian-period warrior transformed by later tales and images into a central demon-slaying hero.
description: Minamoto no Yorimitsu was a historical Heian-period warrior, but the archive follows the much larger figure fashioned by later tales and images. Under the alternate reading Raikō, he becomes the commanding center of a retinue repeatedly sent across the boundary between courtly order and supernatural territory. The Shuten-dōji cycle casts him as expedition leader, strategist, disguised pilgrim, and decapitator; the illustrated Tsuchigumo tale places him beside Watanabe no Tsuna in a haunted sequence of flying skulls, demons, fire, and a monstrous spider. These narrative roles are culturally durable, but they are not treated here as direct evidence for a recoverable historical biography.
traditionNotes: Raikō is an on-reading of the same written name, 源頼光. The archive distinguishes the historical warrior from the supernatural hero assembled across medieval and early-modern tale, theatre, handscroll, and print traditions.

variants.label: Leader of the Mount Ōe expedition

summary: A warrior retainer whose later illustrated legends move between the demon road, the Earth Spider, and the severed-arm encounter.
description: Watanabe no Tsuna is repeatedly pictured at the point where martial reputation meets supernatural instability. Japan Search describes an illustrated tale containing arm-severing and retrieval encounters with disguised opponents, while a separate ColBase record places Tsuna beside Yorimitsu in the haunted sequence that ends with the Earth Spider. A British Museum triptych also names him with Usui Sadamitsu, Urabe no Suetake, and Sakata Kintoki around the Raikō demon-spider tradition. These objects connect him to a retinue without turning their different scenes into one continuous biography.
traditionNotes: The composition of Raikō’s celebrated retainer group and the order, opponent, and setting of Tsuna’s arm tales vary across objects and retellings. Each variant remains attached to the institutional record that describes it.

summary: A named member of Raikō’s retainer tradition whose surviving image-world connects demon-spider combat, watch duty, and supernatural interruption.
description: Institutional collection records identify Usui Sadamitsu among the warriors represented around Minamoto no Yorimitsu. A British Museum triptych names him with Watanabe no Tsuna, Urabe no Suetake, and Sakata Kintoki in an Earth Spider scene. Another museum object preserves a later legend in which Sadamitsu and Kintoki keep watch at Yorimitsu’s residence as conjured goblins interrupt their game of go. Together these works establish a durable visual role within Raikō’s supernatural retinue, but they do not provide a complete or stable life story.
traditionNotes: Usui’s expanded name, companions, and exact actions change across titles and represented objects. This record treats the retainer grouping as a later narrative and visual formation rather than proof of a fixed historical team.

summary: A named warrior in Raikō’s retainer tradition, preserved most clearly here through group images rather than a single unified biography.
description: Urabe no Suetake enters this archive through institutional records that name the companions gathered around Minamoto no Yorimitsu. A Tokyo National Museum actor print catalogued through ColBase identifies Suetake within a Raikō-retainer image, and a British Museum triptych names him beside Usui Sadamitsu, Watanabe no Tsuna, and Sakata Kintoki as Yorimitsu fights the demon spider. The records make his position in the group visible while leaving individual biography and chronology deliberately unresolved.
traditionNotes: The four-retainer label is not visually or narratively identical in every surviving work; some images substitute or rename members. Suetake’s record therefore stays close to named object metadata and does not invent a seamless career.

summary: The later warrior identity associated with Kintarō, represented as a powerful member of Minamoto no Yorimitsu’s retainer tradition.
description: Japan Search presents Kintarō as the childhood name later associated with Sakata no Kintoki and describes the mountain child entering Yorimitsu’s service under the adult name. Institutional prints then place Kintoki among the warriors surrounding Raikō in demon-slaying and Earth Spider scenes. This archive separates the child and adult records so visitors can see the transformation without mistaking every layer of the legend for one documented biography.
traditionNotes: Sources use the written forms 金時 and 公時, and the details of childhood, naming, age, and service belong to layered traditions. The child-to-retainer connection is culturally established in the cited exhibitions, while exact life chronology remains uncertain.
